newsitem.title: USA: Exiles plan landing in Cuba during pope's visit.
newsitem.headline: Exiles plan landing in Cuba during pope's visit.

text.p: An anti-Castro Cuban exile group said on Thursday it planned a series of flotillas to promote a national work stoppage in Cuba and threatened to land exiles on Cuban soil during Pope John Paul II's visit next year.

The Miami-based Democracy Movement announced a non-violent campaign to rally Cubans on the Caribbean island to participate in a massive protest to "persuade or force the present government to yield to a genuine democratization process."

Democracy Movement, which espouses legal, non-violent civil disobedience aimed at forcing Cuban President Fidel Castro to step aside, has run six flotillas of small boats. During one, on July 13, 1995, Cuban military vessels bumped an exile boat, damaging it and injuring several people on board.

The group said it would launch four protest flotillas from U.S. waters in the next 10 months during which exiles could "exercise our right to enter our (Cuban) territorial waters as citizens that were born in that country and who have the right to live in it, regardless of our ideology."

"If such a right is not recognised by the Cuban government prior to the visit of Pope John Paul II, then on the day of his visit to the island we will attempt to land in Cuba ...," Democracy Movement leader Ramon Saul Sanchez told a news conference on Thursday.

But Saul said the group was not trying to provoke an international incident during the pope's visit, scheduled for Jan. 21-25. The visit was agreed to at a historic first meeting last November at the Vatican between the pontiff and Castro.

The exiles assume Cubans on the island hear of their flotillas and other protests one way or another. Prior flotillas and flights by exiles in small planes have been condemned by Cuba as acts of provocation.
Cuban MiG fighters shot down two U.S. civilian aircraft in international airspace between Florida and Cuba on Feb. 24, 1996, killing four members of the exile group Brothers to the Rescue.

The first planned flotilla, on May 17, would promote a national work stoppage, organisers said. They declined to divulge a date for the stoppage, saying it would be revealed when they were sure that most Cubans had heard about the plan.

A flotilla on July 13 will mark the third anniversary of the sinking of the tugboat "13 of March" off the Cuban coast in which 41 people died. Exiles claim the vessel, packed with would-be refugees, was deliberately rammed and sprayed with high-pressure hoses by the Cuban military.

Another flotilla in October would protest the construction of a nuclear power plant in Juragua. Some scientists have said the plant utilizes the same technology as the Soviet Union's Chernobyl plant and could pose a threat to Cuba and Florida.
Movement leaders said they would "reserve, claim or exercise our right" to enter Cuban territory during each of the flotillas.
